PathSnap — Review 1 Report

Distributed map-matching & route reconstruction · UE24CS352A Machine Learning · PES University, RR Campus
Team: [TEAM NAME]  |  Section: G
Members: Vasu Tripathi (PES1UG24AM918), Nidhi S (PES1UG24AM919), Varun ML (PES1UG25AM816), Vinod Kumar L (PES1UG25AM817)
Repository: [GitHub URL]
Summary. GPS fixes are matched to candidate road arcs within 50 m. A classifier scores each (fix, arc) pair, and an HMM with Viterbi decoding turns these scores into a connected route. We compared 7 models from 6 algorithm families with 5-fold trip-grouped CV on the training partition and evaluated them on the 10 student-test trips. LightGBM was selected and tuned with Bayesian optimisation (Optuna TPE, 30 trials). On the student-test trips, tuned LightGBM reaches observation-level Top-1 90.65% and Macro F1 0.9385 as a classifier alone. Phase 2 (Review 2) adds HMM/Viterbi route reconstruction, the FastAPI backend and the evaluator UI.

1. Problem framing and primary metric

Map-matching is cast as candidate classification + sequence decoding. For each GPS observation we collect the directed road arcs within 50 m (up to 8; if none, the 3 nearest within 300 m). A binary classifier then predicts whether each candidate is the reference arc. The primary selection metric is observation-level Top-1 accuracy: for each GPS fix, the highest-scoring candidate is compared with the reference arc. This is exactly what the route output is judged on, and it does not depend on a probability threshold. Candidate-level Macro F1 (threshold 0.5) and log loss are reported as well. Log loss matters because the probabilities become HMM emission scores. Route continuity and route-level arc precision/recall/F1 measure sequence quality.

2. Dataset understanding and EDA

Partitions used. All EDA tables and figures use the train (80 trips) and student_test (10 trips) partitions, labelled in each figure. The evaluator partition was never opened during development. Each trip has its own road network: .nodes (lon, lat), directed .arcs (from, to; row index = arc id) and a .route (ordered arc ids). The .track file holds lon, lat and time in seconds.

Q1. How did we preprocess the data?

(i) Rows with non-finite or out-of-range coordinates are dropped. Timestamps are sorted and de-duplicated; none were found, but the checks run anyway. (ii) Projection: the trips are spread across several continents (see the location plot), so no single UTM zone works. Every trip is projected to a local Azimuthal Equidistant system centred on its GPS centroid, using pyproj. This gives metre units with negligible distortion at trip scale, so Euclidean distance in degrees is never used. (iii) Per-observation reference labels: the .route lists arcs, not one arc per GPS fix. We assign each fix to a route arc with a monotone dynamic-programming alignment, which preserves the order of travel and minimises the total point-to-segment distance. The resulting label distance has median 5.6 m. (iv) Candidate generation uses a KD-tree over arc samples spaced 10 m apart, followed by exact point-to-segment distances. (v) Anomalies: trips 00000033, 00000054 have a systematic GPS-to-network offset (median aligned distance 122 m and 140 m), so the reference arc is almost never within 50 m. These two trips are excluded from model fitting and reported here. (vi) For training only, every 3rd fix is kept, because 1 Hz fixes are highly autocorrelated. Evaluation always uses every fix.

Q2. Patterns observed; features extracted and why

Sampling is nominally 1 Hz: 96.68% of steps are exactly 1 s and 1.96% are 2 s. There are 1216 gaps longer than 5 s in train; the largest is 153064 s, in trip 00000090, and trip 00000078 has 124 such gaps. These motivate the HMM's gap handling. GPS noise is mostly small (median 5.6 m from the aligned arc), but the 95th percentile is 139 m because of the anomalous trips and short outlier bursts. The road networks are large: a mean of 24,169 nodes per training trip. They have no isolated nodes, and the largest strongly connected component covers about 95% of nodes. The reference routes are almost perfectly contiguous head-to-tail. The strongest pattern is that most roads are two-way: each street appears as two opposite arcs at identical distance from the fix. A plain nearest-arc rule therefore gets only 53.24% Top-1 on student-test, and heading features are essential.

Features Why
dist, dist_rank, dist_minus_min, dist_ratio_min Point-to-segment distance and how it compares with the closest candidate – GPS noise is roughly isotropic, so relative distance matters more than absolute distance.
bearing_diff, cos_bearing, ctx_bearing_diff Angle between GPS heading (±2 and ±5 points) and the arc's direction. Arcs are directed and most roads are two-way: two opposite arcs have identical distance, so heading is the only way to choose the right direction (the nearest-arc baseline is only 53.24% Top-1 on student-test for this reason).
ctx_dist_mean, ctx_dist_max Distance of the neighbouring ±3 observations to the same arc – suppresses single-point noise and parallel-road confusion.
proj_t, arc_len Where the projection falls on the arc (end-points indicate junction ambiguity) and arc length.
speed, gps_jump Speed controls how reliable the heading is (stationary vehicles have random headings); jumps flag outliers.
n_cand, is_twoway, out_deg_to, in_deg_from Local road density and junction topology – ambiguity is higher at dense junctions.

Tuned LightGBM's gain importance confirms this design. The top features are dist_minus_min, ctx_bearing_diff and dist_ratio_min: relative distance, heading agreement and context.

3. Model experimentation and comparison

Protocol: 5-fold GroupKFold with trip as the group on the training partition (78 usable trips), so no trip appears in both a training fold and a validation fold. Each model is then refit on all training trips and evaluated once on the 10 student-test trips. Scalers live inside pipelines and are fitted on training data only. The seed is 42 everywhere. Raw logs are in results/model_comparison.csv and results/model_cv_folds.csv.

Selection. LightGBM has the best CV Macro F1, CV Top-1 and CV log loss, and the best student-test Top-1, Macro F1 and log loss. Its fold-to-fold spread is small (±0.011). It trains in about 7 s and needs about 42 ms per 1,000 fixes, which is fast enough for the API. Its well-calibrated probabilities are what the HMM emissions need. XGBoost is a very close second: within about 0.001 on CV Macro F1, CV Top-1 and student-test Top-1, F1 and log loss. RandomForest is next but about 16× slower to train. KNN is competitive in F1 but impractically slow at inference. Logistic regression and Gaussian NB underfit.

3.2 Per-model questions

3.2.1 Model 1: LogisticRegression (Linear / probabilistic)

A1. Why suitable?

A linear, well-calibrated probabilistic baseline. Our features (distance gaps, heading agreement, context distance) are largely monotone with the probability that a candidate is correct, so a linear log-odds model is a reasonable first test and gives a calibrated probability that the HMM can consume directly as an emission score.

A2. Strengths and limitations

Strengths: very fast (sub-millisecond per 1k observations), stable across folds, calibrated probabilities. Limitations: it cannot model interactions such as "heading only matters when speed is high" or the non-linear effect of the bearing difference near 90°, which is where most two-way-road confusions occur.

B5. Important hyperparameters and initial values

C = 1.0 (inverse L2 strength), penalty = L2, solver = lbfgs, max_iter = 2000, StandardScaler fitted inside each training fold.

B6. Loss function / objective

Binary cross-entropy (log loss) with L2 regularisation.

C7. Performance on the student-testing dataset

Observation-level Top-1 87.03%; candidate Macro F1 0.9071 (precision 0.9057, recall 0.9085); raw route continuity 0.711.

C8. Observation-level Top-1, Macro F1 and Log Loss (student test)

Top-1 = 0.8703, Macro F1 = 0.9071, Log Loss = 0.1399 (5-fold CV: Top-1 0.8906 ± 0.0162, Macro F1 0.9107 ± 0.0169).

C9. Overfitting / underfitting?

Train Macro F1 0.9143, CV 0.9107, student test 0.9071. The three are almost identical, so there is no overfitting; the model is underfitting (high bias) – it is about 2.7 Macro-F1 points below the tree ensembles on held-out trips, consistent with the missing feature interactions.

3.2.2 Model 2: GaussianNB (Probabilistic (generative))

A1. Why suitable?

A generative probabilistic model chosen as a contrasting family: it estimates per-class feature distributions and is extremely cheap, which tests whether the features are informative even under a strong independence assumption.

A2. Strengths and limitations

Strengths: trivial to train, no tuning needed, high recall on the positive class. Limitations: the features are strongly correlated (dist, dist_minus_min, dist_ratio_min, ctx_dist_mean all measure distance), which violates the naive independence assumption and double-counts evidence, producing over-confident, poorly calibrated probabilities.

B5. Important hyperparameters and initial values

var_smoothing = 1e-9 (default); no scaling required.

B6. Loss function / objective

Maximum likelihood estimation of class-conditional Gaussian means/variances and class priors (no iterative loss).

C7. Performance on the student-testing dataset

Observation-level Top-1 86.36%; candidate Macro F1 0.8438 (precision 0.8112, recall 0.8987); raw route continuity 0.709.

C8. Observation-level Top-1, Macro F1 and Log Loss (student test)

Top-1 = 0.8636, Macro F1 = 0.8438, Log Loss = 0.5902 (5-fold CV: Top-1 0.8747 ± 0.0187, Macro F1 0.8571 ± 0.0194).

C9. Overfitting / underfitting?

Train Macro F1 0.8585 ≈ CV 0.8571 ≈ test 0.8438 – clear underfitting. Its log loss (0.5902) is 6–7× worse than the boosted models, confirming miscalibration: it has the highest positive-class recall but 9425 false positives on the student test (vs 1821 for LightGBM).

3.2.3 Model 3: KNN (Instance-based)

A1. Why suitable?

An instance-based model: a candidate whose geometry (distance, heading difference, context distance) resembles labelled examples should share their label. It makes no parametric assumption about the decision boundary.

A2. Strengths and limitations

Strengths: non-parametric, captures local non-linear structure. Limitations: sensitive to feature scaling, must store and search the full training set (inference is the slowest of all models), and distance-weighting memorises the training points.

B5. Important hyperparameters and initial values

n_neighbors = 31, weights = distance, metric = Euclidean (Minkowski p=2) on standardised features.

B6. Loss function / objective

None (lazy learner); prediction is the distance-weighted vote of the 31 nearest training candidates.

C7. Performance on the student-testing dataset

Observation-level Top-1 87.30%; candidate Macro F1 0.9196 (precision 0.9242, recall 0.9151); raw route continuity 0.726.

C8. Observation-level Top-1, Macro F1 and Log Loss (student test)

Top-1 = 0.8730, Macro F1 = 0.9196, Log Loss = 0.1588 (5-fold CV: Top-1 0.8878 ± 0.0170, Macro F1 0.9233 ± 0.0110).

C9. Overfitting / underfitting?

Train Macro F1 is 1.0000 (each training point is its own nearest neighbour with infinite weight) versus CV 0.9233 and test 0.9196: it overfits the training points by construction, but generalises reasonably. Its inference cost (3377 ms per 1k observations) makes it impractical for the API.

3.2.4 Model 4: RandomForest (Bagging ensemble)

A1. Why suitable?

A bagging ensemble of decision trees that models non-linear interactions (e.g. bearing difference × speed) and is robust to feature scale and outliers in GPS noise.

A2. Strengths and limitations

Strengths: strong accuracy, low variance across folds, good probability ranking. Limitations: large model files, slowest training of the tree models, and averaged leaf frequencies give slightly less sharp probabilities than boosting.

B5. Important hyperparameters and initial values

n_estimators = 200, max_features = sqrt, min_samples_leaf = 5, bootstrap = True, random_state = 42.

B6. Loss function / objective

Each tree greedily minimises Gini impurity; the forest averages leaf class frequencies.

C7. Performance on the student-testing dataset

Observation-level Top-1 89.48%; candidate Macro F1 0.9340 (precision 0.9409, recall 0.9275); raw route continuity 0.753.

C8. Observation-level Top-1, Macro F1 and Log Loss (student test)

Top-1 = 0.8948, Macro F1 = 0.9340, Log Loss = 0.0920 (5-fold CV: Top-1 0.9024 ± 0.0161, Macro F1 0.9360 ± 0.0099).

C9. Overfitting / underfitting?

Train Macro F1 0.9719 vs CV 0.9360 / test 0.9340: a moderate variance gap (mild overfitting of deep trees), limited by min_samples_leaf = 5; held-out performance is still the second best.

3.2.5 Model 5: LightGBM (Gradient boosting)

A1. Why suitable?

Gradient-boosted trees fit the residual errors sequentially, modelling feature interactions efficiently, and are known to give well-calibrated probabilities with log-loss training – both important for using the scores as HMM emissions.

A2. Strengths and limitations

Strengths: best CV Macro F1, CV Top-1 and log loss among the untuned models, fast training (histogram-based) and fast inference. Limitations: more hyperparameters, can overfit with many leaves, and per-observation predictions are still independent (no sequence context beyond our ±3/±5-point context features).

B5. Important hyperparameters and initial values

n_estimators = 300, learning_rate = 0.05, num_leaves = 31, min_child_samples = 20, subsample = 1.0, colsample_bytree = 1.0, random_state = 42.

B6. Loss function / objective

Binary log loss (cross-entropy) minimised by gradient boosting (second-order, leaf-wise growth).

C7. Performance on the student-testing dataset

Observation-level Top-1 90.49%; candidate Macro F1 0.9388 (precision 0.9409, recall 0.9368); raw route continuity 0.756.

C8. Observation-level Top-1, Macro F1 and Log Loss (student test)

Top-1 = 0.9049, Macro F1 = 0.9388, Log Loss = 0.0874 (5-fold CV: Top-1 0.9051 ± 0.0163, Macro F1 0.9380 ± 0.0106).

C9. Overfitting / underfitting?

Train Macro F1 0.9565 vs CV 0.9380 / test 0.9388. The recorded history (iterations) shows training loss falling from 0.4279 to 0.0668; student-test loss reached its minimum 0.0874 at iteration 298 and ended at 0.0874. Validation loss is still flat-to-decreasing at the last round, so there is no overfitting; the small train/test gap is expected between seen and unseen trips.

3.2.6 Model 6: XGBoost (Gradient boosting)

A1. Why suitable?

A second gradient-boosting implementation (depth-wise trees with regularised objective) to check whether the boosting result is robust to the implementation and tree-growth strategy.

A2. Strengths and limitations

Strengths: accuracy on par with LightGBM, fastest of the boosted models at inference here. Limitations: with a higher learning rate and depth 6 it starts to overfit before 300 rounds; slightly worse CV log loss.

B5. Important hyperparameters and initial values

n_estimators = 300, learning_rate = 0.1, max_depth = 6, tree_method = hist, random_state = 42.

B6. Loss function / objective

Binary log loss with L2 leaf-weight regularisation (λ = 1).

C7. Performance on the student-testing dataset

Observation-level Top-1 90.41%; candidate Macro F1 0.9383 (precision 0.9406, recall 0.9360); raw route continuity 0.769.

C8. Observation-level Top-1, Macro F1 and Log Loss (student test)

Top-1 = 0.9041, Macro F1 = 0.9383, Log Loss = 0.0876 (5-fold CV: Top-1 0.9049 ± 0.0163, Macro F1 0.9368 ± 0.0108).

C9. Overfitting / underfitting?

Train Macro F1 0.9654 vs CV 0.9368 / test 0.9383. The recorded history (iterations) shows training loss falling from 0.3917 to 0.0563; student-test loss reached its minimum 0.0869 at iteration 247 and ended at 0.0876. The rise after the minimum is mild overfitting; early stopping around that round would help.

3.2.7 Model 7: MLP (Neural network)

A1. Why suitable?

A shallow neural network learns non-linear combinations of the standardised features and provides a differentiable alternative to trees, with an epoch-wise training history.

A2. Strengths and limitations

Strengths: smooth decision function, compact model, fast inference. Limitations: needs feature scaling and careful learning-rate/regularisation choices; training is noisier and it did not reach the accuracy of the tree ensembles on these tabular features.

B5. Important hyperparameters and initial values

hidden layers = (64, 32), ReLU, Adam learning_rate_init = 1e-3, alpha (L2) = 1e-4, batch = 512, 25 epochs, StandardScaler.

B6. Loss function / objective

Binary cross-entropy (log loss) with L2 penalty, optimised by Adam mini-batch gradient descent.

C7. Performance on the student-testing dataset

Observation-level Top-1 88.80%; candidate Macro F1 0.9285 (precision 0.9285, recall 0.9286); raw route continuity 0.749.

C8. Observation-level Top-1, Macro F1 and Log Loss (student test)

Top-1 = 0.8880, Macro F1 = 0.9285, Log Loss = 0.1019 (5-fold CV: Top-1 0.8995 ± 0.0164, Macro F1 0.9305 ± 0.0115).

C9. Overfitting / underfitting?

Train Macro F1 0.9470 vs CV 0.9305 / test 0.9285. The recorded history (epochs) shows training loss falling from 0.1110 to 0.0850; student-test loss reached its minimum 0.0997 at epoch 23 and ended at 0.1019. The gap between training and validation loss grows in the later epochs and validation loss fluctuates – mild overfitting plus training instability.

Q3. Objective

mean 3-fold GroupKFold observation Top-1 accuracy, computed on the training partition only. Trial 0 was seeded with the untuned configuration so that the search record contains the baseline. CV Macro F1 and log loss were logged for every trial as user attributes.

Q4. Number of trials

30 trials, sampler TPE (seed 42, 8 random startup trials). Search time was 10.8 min on 2 CPU cores. The full record is in results/bayes_opt_trials.csv.

Q5. Best values

Trial 24 reached an objective of 0.9046, vs 0.9023 for the baseline trial 0. The best values are in the table above.

Q6. Did the tuned model outperform the untuned one?

Metric Untuned LightGBM Tuned LightGBM
CV Macro F1 (5-fold) 0.9380 0.9379
CV Top-1 (5-fold) 0.9051 0.9070
CV Log Loss 0.0929 0.0982
Student-test Top-1 0.9049 0.9065

Only marginally, and only on the metric that was optimised. CV Top-1 rose by +0.19 points and student-test Top-1 by +0.17 points. Raw continuity also improved, from 0.756 to 0.768. Macro F1 was unchanged, and log loss got slightly worse (0.0874 → 0.0892). The tuned trees are larger (num_leaves 155) and more confident. The default configuration was already near the limit of what these features allow. Further gains would have to come from features or the decoder, not from hyperparameters. The tuned model is deployed because it was the pre-registered choice on the CV objective. We did not pick it by looking at student-test results.

8. Limitations, integrity and reproducibility

Reference-label limitations. The per-fix labels come from our monotone alignment of GPS to the .route, so they inherit GPS noise and any route errors. At junctions, and on two-way roads where opposite arcs overlap, a fix's "true" arc is genuinely ambiguous, so Top-1 understates route quality. Two training trips have systematic offsets and were excluded. If such a trip appears at evaluation time, the 50 m candidate radius will often miss the true arc; the 300 m fallback keeps the pipeline running, but accuracy will be low. Leakage control. Splits are trip-grouped. Model and hyperparameter choices used training CV. The evaluator partition was never read, and nothing is hard-coded. Reproducibility. Every number in this report is read by report/build_report.py from results/, and those files are produced by scripts/01–08 with seed 42.
